intro: A manufacturer packing sterile single-use medical products was seeing empty or under-filled packs reach customers, causing complaints and return costs. Hype Vision deployed an inspection station with an industrial camera and controlled lighting that checks every pack with AI.
specs: Hikrobot MV-CT1CG0089 · 8.9 MP, global shutter, GigE

p: Packs were sealed at high speed and operators could only spot-check. On printed sterile packaging, it was hard to tell at a glance whether the product was inside.
Empty or incomplete packs occasionally slipped into shipments, leading to complaints, returns and re-packing costs.

sections.h: Why an industrial camera and lighting?
p: The deciding factor was the image, not the model. A standard CCTV angle and ambient light emphasised the print and hid the content.

A diffuse backlight was placed under the pack. Light passing through the packaging revealed the product's silhouette while suppressing print and reflections. Images were captured with an 8.9 MP global-shutter industrial camera without motion blur.
li: Global shutter: no blur on fast-moving packs
Backlight: clear content silhouette, minimal print effect
Fixed working distance and lens: same scale in every frame
PoE + IP67 housing: suited to the line environment

p: A classification model trained on site footage sorts every pack into PRODUCT OK or EMPTY. The decision is made as the pack enters the field of view and shown with a confidence score.

On EMPTY, a reject signal is sent to the line controller via digital output and the pack is removed automatically. Every decision is logged with a time-stamped image; a pass/reject report per shift is ready in the dashboard.

li: Discovery and sample image collection: 2 days
Camera, lens and lighting installation: 1 day
Model training and field calibration: 5 working days
Parallel run against manual inspection: 2 weeks

p: During the parallel run, system decisions were compared with manual inspection before switching to fully automatic mode.
li: AI model accuracy: 98.6%
Empty/incomplete packs reaching customers: down 94%
Manual final-inspection workload: down 70%
100% inspection at line speed (instead of sampling)
Image evidence for every rejected pack

faq.q: Why an industrial camera instead of existing CCTV?
faq.a: Pack content only became reliably visible with controlled lighting and fixed optics. Existing cameras are enough for safety and operations use cases; product quality inspection usually calls for an industrial camera and lighting.

faq.q: Does it work with different pack sizes?
faq.a: Yes. A new size or print needs only a short sample collection and calibration; one station can run several product recipes.

/vaka-calismalari/kaynak-atolyesi-uretim.title: Digitising a welding shop: welding and grinding time per part, now measured
/vaka-calismalari/kaynak-atolyesi-uretim.desc: At a pipe and flange welding station, an existing IP camera measured welding time, grinding time, cycle time per part, output count and PPE compliance (gloves, face protection) automatically.
intro: At a metal fabrication shop welding pipes, flanges and elbows, production tracking relied on paper forms filled in at the end of the shift. Nobody knew how long a part was welded, how long it was ground or how many minutes a job really took. Hype Vision digitised the process using the existing IP camera that already covered the station.

p: Output and times were written on forms at the end of each shift. How much welding and grinding each part needed, how actively the station was used and whether the times used in quoting were realistic were all unknown.
Glove and face-protection use during welding could only be checked when the HSE specialist walked by.

The station was defined as a region of interest in the camera view. The model detects the welding arc, grinding sparks, gloves, face protection and the workpiece in every frame; tied to time, these detections become operational data.
li: Welding time: total time the arc is on
Grinding time: total time sparks are detected
Cycle time per part: job start → part finished
Output: number of completed parts
Active / idle time: station utilisation during the day
PPE compliance: gloves and face protection while welding and grinding
imgs: Welding — duration counter, gloves and face protection OK
Grinding — spark detection, goggles and gloves OK

p: Each finished part creates a row. A station report is ready at the end of the shift and can be exported to ERP/MES or Excel.
Analysis is station-based; no face recognition is used and nobody is identified. Video is processed on site and only time, count and event data reach the dashboard.
Measured times from the first period were compared with the default times used in planning and costing.
li: Real welding and grinding time per part measured for the first time
Quotes and costing updated with real cycle times
Station utilisation visible per shift
Daily output reported automatically, no paper forms
PPE compliance during welding and grinding logged 24/7

faq.q: Is this tracking individual workers?
faq.a: No. Measurement is station-based: we measure how much welding, grinding and work happened at the station, not who did it. No face recognition is used.

faq.q: Do we need new cameras?
faq.a: This project used the existing IP camera covering the station. If the camera clearly sees the station and the part, no extra hardware is needed.

/vaka-calismalari/maden-tesisi-harman-st.title: 200+ cameras, 20+ modules at a mining plant: product types, forklift time and PPE on one platform
/vaka-calismalari/maden-tesisi-harman-st.desc: At a large mining and chemical plant, more than 200 existing cameras were connected to AI on-premise; product-type zones in the stockyard, forklift operating times and hard-hat use on forklifts are monitored 24/7.
intro: At a large mining and chemical plant where big-bag products are blended and stocked, the stockyard, forklift traffic and HSE rules depended on a few people's eyes. Hype Vision connected more than 200 existing cameras to a single fully on-premise platform and deployed over 20 analytics modules at once.
specs: On-premise · video never leaves the site
Hard hats on forklifts and on site

p: Different product types had to be kept in their own stockyard zones, without mixing, and stock levels had to be known. Checks relied on shift rounds and manual records.
The same area had heavy forklift traffic. How long forklifts worked, waited and where they concentrated was not measured, and hard-hat use by drivers and staff could not be checked continuously.

Each stock zone was defined as a separate area in the camera view (type 1, type 2, type 3). The model detects big-bags and classifies them by zone; a product dropped in the wrong zone or a full zone is reported immediately.
li: Zone-based product-type verification
Alert for products placed in the wrong zone
Zone occupancy and stock movement
Stock records with time-stamped images
imgs: Stockyard — product-type zones and hard-hat check on the forklift driver

p: Forklifts are detected and tracked to measure active work, waiting and time spent in each zone. Hard hats are checked for drivers and staff on the floor; violations trigger alerts with evidence frames.
li: Forklift active and waiting time
Forklift density by zone
Hard-hat check on forklift drivers
Detection of staff without hard hats
imgs: Stock area — hard-hat violation on driver and staff
Blending area — multiple hard-hat violations, tracked with anonymous IDs

p: All analysis runs on servers inside the plant; video never leaves the site. One camera feeds several modules — stock, forklift and PPE analytics from the same image.
More than 20 modules run on the same platform and results land in one dashboard. Nobody is identified; tracking uses anonymous IDs.
Plant-wide inspection moved from rounds and forms to continuous, measurable monitoring.
li: All 200+ cameras on one on-premise platform
20+ modules running concurrently
Product-type mix-ups in the stockyard visible instantly
Forklift usage measurable, planning driven by data
Hard-hat compliance on forklifts and on site logged 24/7
HSE and operations teams work from the same data

faq.q: How much hardware do 200+ cameras need?
faq.a: Hardware is sized during discovery based on camera count, modules and analysis frequency. Since one camera feeds several modules, no device per camera is needed.

faq.q: Does video leave the plant?
faq.a: No. The deployment is on-premise; analysis runs on servers inside the plant and only event and metric data reach the dashboard.

/vaka-calismalari/islak-mendil-skt-baski.title: Expiry date and print inspection on a wet-wipes line: every pack read at line speed
/vaka-calismalari/islak-mendil-skt-baski.desc: On a wet-wipes packaging line, an industrial camera reads and verifies the expiry date, lot and barcode print on every pack; packs with missing, faded or shifted print are rejected. The system runs on-premise on a closed network.
intro: At a wet-wipes plant, the expiry date, lot number and barcode printed on every pack had to be legible and correct. Checks relied on operators pulling packs at intervals. Hype Vision installed an industrial camera and lighting at the packaging outfeed to inspect every pack's print at line speed.

p: On glossy, wrinkled packaging the expiry and lot print sometimes came out faded, incomplete, shifted or with the wrong date. Sampling missed some of these packs, which could end up in shipments.
A wrong or unreadable expiry date means recall, complaint and regulatory risk.

Foil packaging reflects light, so consistent reading with a standard camera wasn't possible. A global-shutter industrial camera and glare-suppressing diffuse lighting were placed at the outfeed, capturing the print area at the same scale and sharpness in every frame.
li: Global shutter: no blur on fast-moving packs
Diffuse light: foil glare suppressed
Fixed optics: same reading area on every pack
Triggered capture: one frame per pack
imgs: Pack print area — expiry, lot and barcode lines read and verified

p: AI-powered OCR reads the lines in the print area and compares them with the shift's production order. The print itself is also assessed: missing characters, faded print, shifts or smears are detected.
li: Is the expiry date correct and in the right format?
Does the lot number match the production order?
Is the barcode readable and correct?
Is the print missing, faded, shifted or smeared?
Reject signal and image record for defective packs

p: The system runs entirely inside the plant on a closed network with no internet connection. Images and records never leave the site; production order data comes from the local system and results are written to a local dashboard.
Once live, print inspection moved from sampling to 100% inspection.
li: Expiry and lot print checked on every pack at line speed
Packs with defective print rejected automatically before shipping
Time-stamped image for every rejected pack
Less manual inspection for operators
Digital evidence archive of print quality for audits

faq.q: Does it work with different products and packs?
faq.a: Yes. The reading area and expected format are defined once per product; on changeover the operator selects the recipe.

faq.q: Is an internet connection required?
faq.a: No. In this project the system runs on a closed network, fully on-premise.

/vaka-calismalari/paketleme-hatti-yogunl.title: Density and bottleneck analysis on packing lines: which station slows the line?
/vaka-calismalari/paketleme-hatti-yogunl.desc: At a fresh-produce packing plant, existing cameras measured unit counts, active working time and line density per station; bottleneck stations and hours were identified with data.
intro: At a plant sorting and boxing fresh vegetables, line capacity was the same on paper, yet end-of-day box counts differed widely between stations. Nobody knew which point was slowing the line. Hype Vision used the existing cameras covering the lines to measure how much each station processed and how actively it worked.

p: Belt speed was set the same for the whole line, but product piled up at some stations while staff waited idle at others. Only the total box count was known at the end of the shift; where time was lost was invisible.

Each station was defined as a product area (ROI) in the camera view. Products moving from the area into boxes are counted; anonymous pose analysis separates active working time from waiting. Product density on the belt is measured from the same image.
li: Products / boxes per station
Active work vs. idle waiting time
Product density and build-up on the belt
Hourly throughput curve and shift comparison
imgs: Boxing station — product area, counter and anonymous pose analysis

p: Placing every station's hourly throughput side by side clearly showed that certain stations and hours were holding up the rest of the line. Product build-up on the belt rose in the same time windows.
Staffing and belt layout at the bottleneck stations were re-planned based on the data.
li: Bottleneck stations and hours identified with data
Staffing re-planned according to station load
Line density and build-up monitored live
Shift and day comparisons reported automatically
Station-based measurement without tracking individuals

faq.q: Are individual workers tracked?
faq.a: No. Measurement is station-based; pose analysis only determines whether work is happening at the station, and nobody is identified.

faq.q: Do we need new cameras?
faq.a: Existing cameras that see the lines from above are usually enough; camera angles are reviewed during discovery.

/vaka-calismalari/tir-yukleme-sevkiyat-s.title: Automatic shipment counting at the truck loading dock: every load, every vehicle on record
/vaka-calismalari/tir-yukleme-sevkiyat-s.desc: An existing camera covering the dock detects the trailer and forklift automatically; loads entering the trailer are counted and shipment quantity and video evidence are matched against the order.
intro: At a plant's dispatch dock, the quantity loaded into each truck was counted by hand at the end of loading and compared with the delivery note. Short or over-loading was only noticed at the customer, with no evidence for disputes. Hype Vision started counting and recording loading automatically using the existing camera covering the dock.
specs: Editable ROI or automatic trailer detection

p: Counting depended on the operator; at busy times or shift changes numbers could get mixed up. For customer 'short delivery' claims there was no footage, and it was unclear whether the issue came from loading or transport.
The trailer's rear door is used as the counting zone (ROI). It can be a fixed zone defined per dock and editable in the dashboard, or detected automatically each time a new truck backs in.

The forklift and its load are tracked; when a load enters the trailer zone and the forklift leaves empty, the counter increments. Reverse movements are subtracted. Every count is saved with that moment's image.
li: Automatic trailer and rear-door detection
Counting zone (ROI) editable in the dashboard
Forklift + load tracking for in/out direction
Loading start–end time per vehicle
imgs: Forklift approaching the trailer with a load · count 2
Load entered the trailer zone · count 3

p: Load count, duration and evidence frames are collected in one shipment record per vehicle and compared with the order quantity in the delivery note or ERP; any difference triggers an alert before the truck leaves.
Shipment counting moved from a manual task to an automatic, evidence-backed process.
li: Automatic load count per vehicle
Order vs. loaded differences caught before the truck leaves
Video evidence for customer claims
Dock utilisation and loading times measured
No more manual counting or count sheets

faq.q: Does each dock need separate setup?
faq.a: The zone is defined once per dock camera; with automatic trailer detection, counting continues even if the truck position changes.

faq.q: Can loose items be counted, not just pallets?
faq.a: Yes; the model is trained per product type. Rolls, sacks, cartons or pallets can be counted separately.

/vaka-calismalari/fuar-ziyaretci-yogunlu.title: Visitor density and aisle analytics at a trade fair: which stand, how many people, how long?
/vaka-calismalari/fuar-ziyaretci-yogunlu.desc: At an international fair, existing cameras measured live and total visitors, peak density and dwell time in aisles, stand fronts, seating and waiting zones — anonymously.
intro: At a large fair, exhibitors and the organiser could only guess which areas really drew interest. Hype Vision split the hall into zones using the cameras covering it and measured visitor flow anonymously throughout the event.

p: Stand success was judged by guest books and impressions. Which aisle was crowded, which stand people passed without stopping and how much seating was used were unknown. The organiser's safety and flow planning was also guesswork.

The hall view was split into aisles, stand fronts, seating and transit/waiting zones. For each zone the live count, total visitors, daily peak and average dwell time are calculated; density level (low / medium / high) is shown live.
li: Live, total and peak people count
Average dwell time per zone
Density level and hourly curve
Aisle flow and direction
Stop rate in front of stands
imgs: 5-zone KPI panel · aisle, stand front, seating and waiting areas
Stand entrance and aisle · dwell time per person

p: Exhibitors see how many visitors passed and stopped, peak hours and average attention time, and judge their fair investment with data. The organiser monitors aisle density live for safety, guidance and next year's layout.
No face recognition is used and nobody is identified. People are counted with temporary anonymous IDs that are never linked to a person or stored. Only count and time data reach the dashboard.
Floor usage became measurable for the first time across the event.
li: Hourly and daily visitor data per zone
Stop and dwell times at stand fronts
Aisle bottlenecks and peak hours identified
Data for the organiser's layout and safety planning
Anonymous, privacy-compliant measurement

faq.q: Are visitors' faces recorded?
faq.a: No. Analysis is anonymous; only count and time data are produced.

faq.q: Can this work in stores and malls?
faq.a: Yes; the same method applies to retail, malls, museums and event venues for visitor flow and zone usage.

/vaka-calismalari/acik-alan-duman-tespit.title: Early smoke detection outdoors: the camera sees where detectors can't reach
/vaka-calismalari/acik-alan-duman-tespit.desc: Around a mining and silo site, existing perimeter cameras detected smoke at an early stage with AI and raised alerts with evidence frames.
intro: At a site surrounded by silos, stockyards, a motorway verge and grassland, a small outdoor fire or smoke was noticed late in areas without smoke detectors. Hype Vision turned the perimeter cameras already installed for security into an early-warning smoke detection system.

p: Point smoke detectors are for indoor spaces and don't work in open, windy areas. Perimeter cameras only recorded, and nobody watched screens 24/7. Smoke starting in dry grass could grow within minutes.

The AI model was trained to distinguish smoke plumes and flames from ground, sky and dust. A detection is confirmed over several frames before becoming an alert, so brief dust, fog or exhaust doesn't cause false alarms.
Alerts are sent to the control-room dashboard and mobile devices with camera name, location, time and a marked evidence frame.
li: Outdoor smoke and flame detection
Multi-frame confirmation to reduce false alarms
Zone-based sensitivity (stockyard, grassland, roadside)
Instant alert with evidence frame
imgs: Silo site perimeter · smoke starting outdoors flagged at an early stage

p: Early warning lets a small plume be put out before it becomes a fire. Since existing cameras are used, no new sensors, cabling or infrastructure are needed, and the same cameras keep doing perimeter security.
Perimeter cameras moved from passive recording to active early warning.
li: 24/7 smoke monitoring in outdoor areas without detectors
Smoke detected at the first stage and sent to the team
Every alert logged with an evidence frame
No new sensors or cabling required

faq.q: Does it replace smoke detectors?
faq.a: No. Vision-based detection is a complementary layer; it doesn't replace legally required fire detection, but adds early warning especially outdoors where detectors don't exist.

faq.q: Do fog or dust trigger false alarms?
faq.a: Multi-frame confirmation and site-specific calibration keep such false alarms to a minimum.

/vaka-calismalari/400-kamera-alan-bazli-.title: Zone-based PPE monitoring on 400 cameras: hard hats, vests, safety shoes and gloves
/vaka-calismalari/400-kamera-alan-bazli-.desc: At a large production and warehousing site, hard-hat and vest monitoring went live on 400 cameras; safety-shoe and glove checks were added at entrance gates, with separate PPE rules per zone.
intro: At a site with many halls, warehouse aisles and entrance gates, the HSE team couldn't check PPE compliance across the whole site at once. Hype Vision connected all 400 cameras to a single PPE platform and defined rules that check the equipment each zone requires.

p: Different zones required different PPE: hard hat and vest in production halls, vest in warehouse aisles, safety shoes and gloves at some entrances. HSE staff inspected by walking rounds and most violations went unseen. There was no systematic record for audits.

sections.h: Hard hats and vests on 400 cameras
p: All 400 cameras were connected to one platform with hard-hat and hi-vis vest checks running on every camera. A violation creates a popup alert in the dashboard and VMS with camera, location, time and a marked evidence frame.
li: Concurrent hard-hat and vest checks on 400 cameras
VMS popup and mobile alerts
Time-stamped violation archive
Compliance report by shift and zone
imgs: Warehouse aisle · PPE detection and VMS popup alert

sections.h: Safety shoes and gloves at entrance gates
p: Rules were extended on cameras at gates leading into production: in addition to the hard hat, safety shoes and gloves are checked. Non-compliant entries are flagged instantly and can be integrated with turnstiles or door locks.
li: Safety-shoe check at entry
Glove check at entry
Multi-PPE rule together with hard hat
Ready for turnstile / door integration
imgs: Entrance gate · compliant PPE (left) and entry without safety shoes (middle, right)

p: A separate PPE rule is defined per camera and zone; which equipment is mandatory where is managed in the dashboard. A vest is enough in a warehouse aisle, a face shield is required in welding, safety shoes at the gate — no unnecessary alerts.
PPE monitoring moved from sampled rounds to continuous coverage of the whole site.
li: 24/7 hard-hat and vest monitoring on 400 cameras
Safety-shoe and glove checks at entrance gates
Separate PPE rules per zone, no unnecessary alerts
Violations reach the VMS with evidence frames
Systematic digital record for HSE audits

faq.q: Do 400 cameras run on a single server?
faq.a: Hardware is sized by camera count and modules; large deployments combine several edge servers in one dashboard.

faq.q: Are people identified?
faq.a: No. PPE monitoring is anonymous; only the presence of equipment is checked and no face recognition is used.
